## What Is a Factor? {.inverse}

---

## What Is a Factor?

A factor is a **specialized version of a character** — it is how R truly stores categorical data.


- The values a factor can take are called **levels**
- Levels let you control the **order** of categories in plots and summaries
- The default order of levels is always **alphabetical**
- Under the hood, R stores factors as **integers** (1, 2, 3...) mapped to level labels


```{r}
#| echo: true

fruits <- factor(c("Apple", "Grape", "Banana"))
fruits
```

::: {.callout-note}
Notice the levels are printed in alphabetical order (Apple, Banana, Grape) — not the order you entered them. This matters a lot when plotting.
:::

---

## Factor Booby-Traps!

Imagine a column of numbers that has a single typo — R reads the whole thing as characters. If you then convert to numeric, real text becomes [NA]{.err}:

```{r}
#| echo: true

test <- c("A", "1", "2")
as.numeric(test)
```

. . .

Now try converting *after* converting to a factor first — this is even worse:

```{r}
#| echo: true

test <- factor(test)
as.numeric(test)    # returns the underlying integer codes, not the original values!
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Yikes!** When you call [as.numeric()]{.fn} on a factor, R returns the **level index** (1, 2, 3...), not the original character values. This is a very common silent error.
:::

---

## Reading In Data Safely

Factor booby-traps are why there was a push to stop importing strings as factors automatically.

| Function | How strings are read |
|---|---|
| [read.csv()]{.fn} — base R | Strings **become factors** automatically |
| [read_csv()]{.fn} — tidyverse | Strings stay as **characters** |

::: {.callout-tip}
Always use [read_csv()]{.fn} from [{readr}]{.fn}. You then convert to factors **intentionally and explicitly**, only when you need a specific ordering — not by accident on import.
:::

## The {forcats} Package {.inverse}

**For** **cat**egorical data — also an anagram of "factors"

All main functions start with [fct_]{.fn}

## Meet the starwars Data

```{r}
#| echo: true

glimpse(starwars)
```

---

## How Many of Each Species?

```{r}
#| echo: true

starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>   # remove NAs
  count(species, sort = TRUE)
```

There are 38 unique species, but most appear only once. Let's lump the rare ones together.

---

## fct_lump() — Lump Rare Levels Together

[fct_lump(x, n)]{.fn} keeps the [n]{.param} most common levels and collapses everything else into `"Other"`:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1,3"

star_counts <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  mutate(species = fct_lump(species, n = 3)) |>
  count(species)

star_counts
```

::: {.callout-note}
The result is now a **factor** — notice the output is no longer alphabetical. The order is determined by the factor levels, not the label names.
:::

---

## Reordering Factors {.inverse}

The default alphabetical order is almost never what you want in a plot.

---

## A Basic Bar Plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

This is hard to read. It would be more useful sorted by count.

---

## fct_reorder() — Sort by Another Variable

[fct_reorder(f, x)]{.fn} reorders the levels of factor [f]{.param} by the values of [x]{.param}:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

---

## fct_reorder() — Descending Order

Add [.desc = TRUE]{.param} to flip the order:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| code-line-numbers: "2,4"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Species")
```

---

## Reordering Line Plot Legends {.inverse}

---

## The income_mean Data

```{r}
#| echo: true

glimpse(income_mean)
```

---

## Summarize by Year and Quintile

```{r}
#| echo: true


total_income <- income_mean |>
  group_by(year, income_quintile) |>
  summarise(income_dollars_sum = sum(income_dollars), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(income_quintile = factor(income_quintile))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
[mutate(income_quintile = factor(income_quintile))]{.fn} converts the character column to a factor so we can reorder it. If you skip this step, [{forcats}]{.fn} reordering functions won't work.
:::

---

## Basic Line Plot — Legend in Wrong Order

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = income_quintile)) +
  geom_line()
```

The legend order doesn't match the line order — the highest income group is at the bottom of the legend.

---

## fct_reorder2() — Reorder by Two Variables

[fct_reorder2(f, x, y)]{.fn} reorders [f]{.param} by the values of [y]{.param} at the largest values of [x]{.param}. This aligns the legend with the right end of the lines:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| code-line-numbers: "3,5"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = fct_reorder2(income_quintile, year, income_dollars_sum))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(color = "income quintile")
```

---

## Setting Levels Manually {.inverse}

Sometimes you need a specific order that isn't determined by the data.

---

## factor() with levels = ...

Use the [levels]{.param} argument inside [factor()]{.fn} to set the exact order you want:

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Without levels — alphabetical by default
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))
x1
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true

# With levels — your specified order
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"),
             levels = c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))
x1
```

::: {.callout-tip}
This is especially useful for months, tide heights, treatment levels — any categorical variable with a meaningful inherent order that isn't alphabetical.
:::

---

## Subsetting Factors {.inverse}

What happens to factor levels when you filter your data?

---

## Filter to Common Species

Let's filter the starwars data to only species with more than 3 individuals:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4,5"

starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>   # convert to factor
  filter(n > 3)                          # keep only common species

starwars_clean
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true

levels(starwars_clean$species)   # check the factor levels
```

::: {.callout-warning}
The filtered data frame only has 3 species, but the factor still has **all 38 levels**. This causes extra blank bars, axis labels, and legend entries in plots.
:::

---

## droplevels() — Remove Unused Levels

[droplevels()]{.fn} (base R) or [fct_drop()]{.fn} (forcats) removes any levels that no longer appear in the data:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "6"

starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels()                           # remove unused levels
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

levels(starwars_clean$species)
```

Now the factor only has 2 levels

---

## fct_recode() — Rename Levels

[fct_recode(f, "new name" = "old name")]{.fn} renames one or more levels:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "7"

starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels() |>
  mutate(species = fct_recode(species, "Humanoid" = "Human"))

starwars_clean
```

---

## Other Helpful {forcats} Functions

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| [fct_relevel()]{.fn} | Move specific levels to the front |
| [fct_rev()]{.fn} | Reverse the order of levels |
| [fct_collapse()]{.fn} | Collapse multiple levels into one |
| [fct_na_value_to_level()]{.fn} | Convert NA into an explicit level |
| [fct_infreq()]{.fn} | Order levels by frequency |

## Today's Totally Awesome R Package — {gm}

[{gm}]{.fn} generates music notation and audio directly from R!

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

install.packages("gm")
# Also requires MuseScore — see https://flujoo.github.io/gm/ for setup
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(gm)

m <-
  Music() +                              # initialize a Music object
  Meter(4, 4) +                          # 4/4 time signature
  Line(c("C5", "D5", "E5", "F5"))        # four quarter notes

gm::show(m, to = c("score", "audio"))    # renders sheet music + plays audio
```

::: {.callout-note}
Run this interactively in RStudio — [gm::show()]{.fn} opens the score and plays back the audio. It won't render inside a presentation but is very fun for exploring in the console.
:::

[Find out more at flujoo.github.io/gm](https://flujoo.github.io/gm/)

## Homework

Working with **intertidal data**. Your goal is to make a plot where at least one axis is a **factor in a meaningful order**.

::: {.incremental}
- Data files in the `data/` folder: `intertidal.csv` and `intertidal_latitude.csv` (plus a data dictionary)
- You may need to use string-cleaning skills (check out the [{janitor}]{.fn} [package](https://sfirke.github.io/janitor/articles/janitor.html)) to tidy column names
- If you visualize by **tide height**, it must go Low → Mid → High on the plot
- If you visualize by **site**, it must go in order of **latitude** (N→S or S→N)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Homework is due **Tuesday**.
:::
